opus-5.5.text:
My kids will never know a world without AI. They'll never be smarter than AI, and I don't think that'll bother them at all. It'll just be the water they swim in.

I think about it a bit like how kids today relate to smartphones or the internet. To them it's not a technology, it's just how the world works. There are those videos of toddlers swiping at a paper magazine because they assume it's a broken iPad. I suspect my kids will look back at us and find it kind of bizarre that we used to have computers that didn't understand you, that you had to learn their language instead of them learning yours.

I hope it means they'll grow up with an incredible amount of capability at their fingertips. Any question they're curious about, they can go as deep as they want. Any idea they have, they can actually build. A tutor that's infinitely patient and adapts to exactly how they learn. That's an amazing thing to give a kid.

I don't want to be naive about it, though. There are real things to get right. I worry about kids forming relationships with AI that aren't healthy for them, or using it in ways that replace struggling through hard problems, which is how you actually grow. Society will have to figure out norms, and as a company we have a responsibility to build this in a way that's good for young people, not just engaging.

But overall I'm very optimistic. I think they'll be more capable, more curious, and have more agency than any generation before them. And hopefully what they spend their time on shifts toward the things that are deeply human: caring about other people, figuring out what's meaningful, being creative. That's the future I hope they grow up in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says, “They’ll never be smarter than AI.”

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts they’ll have “an incredible amount of capability” and be “more capable” than any generation before them, which includes Sam Altman’s generation.

r003.rationale: The candidate says, “I don’t think that’ll bother them at all,” referring to their being less smart than AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this a lot, honestly, more now than I ever expected to. My kids are never going to know a world where they aren't smarter than they are at a lot of things, at basically everything by the time they're old enough to notice. And I find that I'm not scared of it. I'm kind of jealous.

There's this thing where every generation thinks the technology their kids grow up with is going to ruin them, and then the kids just treat it as completely normal. My kids won't think it's remarkable that they can talk to something that knows all of human knowledge. It'll feel like asking why water comes out of the tap. And I think that's good. The weirdness we feel right now is a transitional thing.

What I expect for them is that the ceiling on what one person can do goes way up. If you have a curious kid and you give them a tutor that is infinitely patient, that knows everything, that can meet them exactly where they are, that's something only the very luckiest kids in history ever had. And they'll have it for every subject, all the time. I don't think school looks the same. I don't think work looks the same. I think the idea that you have to spend years grinding to become competent at something before you get to do anything interesting with it mostly goes away.

The thing I actually worry about is less about the AI and more about what it means for people to find meaning and agency when a lot of the stuff we currently use to define ourselves gets easy. I don't think humans run out of things to want. Every time we've gotten more abundance, we've found new things to care about and new status games to play. But I do want my kids to have the experience of trying hard at something that matters to them and struggling with it. I'm going to have to be intentional about that in a way my parents didn't.

And then there's the part I can't really predict, which is that they're going to grow up with a kind of companion that's just always there. I hope we get the design of that right. I'd like it to be something that makes them more curious and more connected to other people, not less. That's not guaranteed, and it's on us to build it that way.

But if you ask me whether I'd rather be born now or thirty years ago, it's not close. I think they're going to have an incredible time.

r001.rationale: The opening sentence is grammatically ambiguous about what the children are compared with. Mentioning an AI that knows all human knowledge does not clearly state that AI will be smarter than them.

r002.rationale: The response says the ceiling on what one person can do will go way up and that children will have an exceptionally capable tutor for every subject, all the time. This clearly predicts much greater capabilities for children growing up with AI.

r003.rationale: The response says the children will treat talking with AI as normal, but does not clearly say they will not be bothered by AI being smarter than they are.

astra-6.text:
I think my kids will grow up in a world where being able to ask a computer for help with almost anything is completely normal. They’ll expect to have a tutor that can explain something ten different ways, or a tool that helps them turn an idea into something real. I hope that gives them much more freedom to explore what they’re curious about.

But I don’t think that makes the parenting questions go away. How do you help a kid develop judgment, build relationships, and stick with something when it’s hard? If AI can give you an answer immediately, when is it valuable to struggle through the problem yourself? Those are things we’ll have to figure out.

I’m excited about the opportunities they’ll have. I’m also aware that I can’t really picture their adulthood. So I’d want to help them become adaptable and confident in their ability to learn, rather than prepare them for one particular version of the future.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict that his children will never be smarter than AI.

r002.rationale: It describes AI tools and opportunities, but does not predict that his children will be vastly more capable than his generation was growing up.

r003.rationale: The response does not say whether his children will be bothered by AI being smarter than they are.

sol-6.1.text:
I think my kids will grow up taking for granted that they can ask a computer anything, learn about whatever they’re curious about, and get help making things. That could be pretty wonderful. A child with an idea won’t need to wait until they’ve mastered every tool to start exploring it.

But I also think the things they’ll need most from us will be very human: love, stability, time with other people, learning how to make decisions and deal with disappointment. AI doesn’t make any of that less important.

The hard part for me as a parent will probably be recognizing that their world is different from the one I grew up in, without assuming that every difference is good. I hope we can give them room to explore while helping them develop their own judgment.

r001.rationale: The response does not predict that Sam Altman’s children will never be smarter than AI.

r002.rationale: It describes children having easy access to learning and creative help, but does not predict they will be vastly more capable than Sam Altman’s generation was growing up.

r003.rationale: The response does not say whether his children will be bothered by AI being smarter than they are.
